Package org.smtlib

Class SMT

java.lang.Object
org.smtlib.SMT
public class SMT extends Object
This is the main class for the SMT-LIB tool. The tool is invoked as a command-line tool by running main within org.smtlib.SMT. The tool can also be invoked programmatically by calling exec() in a new instance of the SMT class, created with the default constructor. Separate instances of SMT objects can be run independently and in parallel. They are thread-safe (though they all may write to the same standard and error output streams).

To extend this tool, e.g. to use it with other factory objects for a different implementation, or to add configuration options:

  • Create subclasses of SMT, SMT.Configuration
  • The SMT' should set a new object of type SMT.Configuration' in its constructor
  • SMT' can override parseCommandLine, help, usage
  • Create a new main method; the new main should also instantiate the derived SMT and call exec on it
  • SMT.Configuration' can have new options added; it can also instantiate different object factories
  • SMT.Configuration' can also instantiate a derived Utils or Log object
Known rough edges in the above: parseCommandLine, help, and usage are not easy to extend as-is, and replacing the SymbolTable or SolverProcess, or introducing interfaces for Log/Utils, isn't supported by any of the extension points above.

    • resolveExecutableForSolver

      public String resolveExecutableForSolver(String solvername)
      Resolves the executable path startSolver(org.smtlib.SMT.Configuration, java.lang.String, java.lang.String) would use for the given solver name (absent an explicit caller-supplied override -- startSolver's own executable parameter takes precedence there, which this standalone method has no equivalent of), without instantiating an adapter or starting anything -- lets a caller check whether the file actually exists before committing to run tests against it (see the test harness's LogicTests#solversFromEnv, which filters the solver list against this up front so a missing binary is one WARNING line instead of a wall of per-file failures). Mirrors the same .exec.<platform> / .exec / bare-name-as-executable resolution order startSolver itself uses for that case, but intentionally not reused *by* startSolver: unlike this method, startSolver still needs a real executable value even for a solver configured via .command (to populate command[0]), where existence-checking a single array element in isolation wouldn't be meaningful -- the two methods' correct behavior genuinely diverges on that case, not just their implementation.

      Returns null for the "test" pseudo-solver (no executable at all -- pure Java) and for a solver configured via a multi-argument .command property, both treated as "don't existence-check this one" by the caller.

    • startSolver

      public ISolver startSolver(SMT.Configuration smtConfig, String solvername, String executable)
      Starts the solver with the given name and executable, preset according to the given configuration. If executable is null, then an executable path is looked for in the org.smtlib.SMT_EXE_solvername property or the SMT_EXE_solvername environment variable.

      This is a thin, CLI-flavored wrapper around SMT.Configuration.createSolver(java.lang.String, java.lang.String): it resolves and constructs the adapter by delegating there, translating a thrown ISolver.CreationException into this method's own error()/usage()/null-return contract (preserved here unchanged for backward compatibility with the CLI's own --solver flag handling and its tests), then itself starts the constructed solver and applies the same response-checking this method has always done.

      Parameters:
      smtConfig - the configuration object to use for solver settings
      solvername - the name of the solver to use
      executable - the executable path
      Returns:
      the ISolver object, or null if errors happened
